items.title: The most important question you’ll ask 1,000 times a day
items.description:
You are able to make good decisions about how to live your life. 
 I hate to open a new newsletter with a twee self-help aphorism covered in fortune cookie crumbs, but it’s probably the most important thing to start with. Because Epicureanism is an ancient Greek philosophy, and like almost all its contemporaries, it places responsibility on  you . You are the overseer of your life. items.title: How to navigate the world with two halves of one brain
items.description:
Psychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent 35 years studying how the brain shapes consciousness. In this full interview, he explains why the two hemispheres attend to the world in radically different ways, and how one narrow, grasping mode has come to dominate Western civilization. He then explores the nature of reality: a creative cosmos that flows at the edge of chaos, where consciousness is primary and matter is one of its phases. He closes with what makes a human life flourish.

items.title: The surprising science of awe — and what it reveals about consciousness
items.description:
Years ago on the way to New Zealand for my doctoral studies, I stopped in Los Angeles to visit a friend. He organized a trip to Joshua Tree, where we hiked and camped. Come nightfall, I gazed at the stars and clouds — or so I thought. My friend pointed out that the cloudcover was, in fact, the Milky Way.

items.title: NASA’s next flagship to answer the biggest question: “Are we alone?”
items.description:
There are a few questions that humanity has always pondered, yet scarcely could satisfactorily answer until the proper scientific advances came along. Questions like: 
 
 What is the Universe? 
 Where did it come from? 
 How did it get to be this way? 
 And what is its ultimate fate?

items.title: Made in Our Image: A Live Conversation on AI
items.description:
Big Think hosted a live event on our latest issue,  Made in Our Image , which explores the philosophies behind artificial intelligence and what they reveal about us. Executive Producer Dan Hayes sat down with the writers behind the magazine for a candid conversation about the human side of this century’s most consequential technology, along with a behind-the-scenes look at what went into making our favorite issue yet.

items.title: Why everyone should be doing therapy
items.description: I would bet my house that you’re living with something. There is some sickness, pain, or condition you’ve learned to deal with. Because there is no such thing as “perfect” health. Everyone you talk to, everyone you see on the street, everyone in the line at the coffee shop, has something they have to adapt to. items.title: The black hole information paradox
items.description:
In 1915, an astronomer stationed on the Russian front was supposed to be calculating artillery trajectories. Instead, Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein’s new equations of general relativity before Einstein himself could, and in doing so he uncovered the math of black holes, objects Einstein spent decades insisting could not exist. Physicist Brian Greene, author of The Elegant Universe and Until the End of Time, uses black holes as a sledgehammer to test what we really know about reality.

items.title: How Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day
items.description: As of November 18, 2026, if you send a signal out at the speed of light in the direction of Voyager 1 — humanity’s most distant spacecraft — it will now  take more than a full day for that signal to arrive . items.title: Did men evolve to fight each other? Scientists can’t agree.
items.description:
Anthropologist David Puts was a graduate student trying to decide on a dissertation topic when inspiration struck him at a mall food court.
